report:
**Conclusion:** Your sister’s claim is *plausible but too broad as stated*. The best evidence supports improving **bedroom ventilation**—not necessarily opening a particular window or door—as one way to modestly improve sleep and next-day functioning, especially in a stuffy, poorly ventilated bedroom.

A randomized crossover study found that lowering bedroom CO₂ (a useful marker of inadequate ventilation and occupants’ exhaled air) significantly improved objectively measured sleep quality, perceived air freshness, next-day sleepiness, concentration, and logical-thinking performance. Ventilation was altered without meaningful temperature differences between conditions. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/

There is direct, but limited, evidence on openings: a field intervention involving **17 healthy young adults** examined window/door opening, bedroom ventilation, and sleep. Its small size, narrow participant group, and real-world setting mean it supports an association/intervention effect but cannot establish that everyone will benefit equally. https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/windowdoor-opening-mediated-bedroom-ventilation-and-its-impact-on/

The broader research base remains limited. A review notes relatively little evidence on bedroom ventilation’s consequences for sleep and next-day performance, so claims that an open window or door is “proven” to improve sleep for all people overstate the science. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132320306004

**Important caveat:** An open window can also admit road noise, which itself is associated with poorer self-rated sleep. Thus, opening it may help in a quiet, safe area with clean/cool outdoor air, but could hurt sleep in a noisy, polluted, very hot/cold, or unsafe setting. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34043056/

Practical takeaway: prioritize a comfortably cool, quiet bedroom with adequate fresh-air exchange; use an open window/door only if its trade-offs are favorable.
